notes.definition: Everyday electrical appliances are designed to transfer energy from batteries or the a.c. mains to useful stores, such as the kinetic store of a motor or the thermal store of a heating element. The energy transferred depends on the power and how long the appliance is on: E = P t. Work is done when charge flows through a potential difference: E = Q V.
explanation: Electrical appliances are designed to bring about energy transfers. When an appliance is switched on, charge flows through it and work is done: energy is transferred electrically from the supply (the chemical store of a battery, or the a.c. mains supplied by a power station) to the appliance. The appliance then transfers this energy to another store. In an electric kettle, the heating element transfers energy to the thermal store of the water. In a fan, food mixer or drill, an electric motor transfers energy to a kinetic store. A hair dryer does both: a heating element warms the air and a motor drives the fan.

The amount of energy an appliance transfers depends on its power and how long it is switched on. Energy transferred = power × time, E = P t, with E in joules (J), P in watts (W) and t in seconds (s). A 2 kW heater left on for one hour transfers twice as much energy as a 1 kW heater on for the same time, and the same 2 kW heater left on for two hours transfers twice as much again.

The energy transferred can also be found from the charge that flows and the potential difference: energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference, E = Q V, with Q in coulombs (C) and V in volts (V). This is because potential difference is the energy transferred per unit charge: a potential difference of 230 V means each coulomb transfers 230 J. Combining E = Q V with Q = I t gives E = V I t, which links back to P = V I.

Before substituting, convert to standard units. Change kilowatts to watts by multiplying by 1000. Change minutes to seconds (× 60) and hours to seconds (× 3600). Energies are often large, so you may give answers in kilojoules (1 kJ = 1000 J) or megajoules (1 MJ = 1 000 000 J).

Power ratings let you compare appliances. A kettle rated at 3000 W transfers 3000 J to the thermal store of the water every second, so it boils water much faster than a 1000 W travel kettle. The higher the power rating, the faster the energy in the appliance's useful store changes. Not all the energy is transferred usefully: some is dissipated to the surroundings, for example as sound from a motor or heating of the casing.
keyFacts: Appliances transfer energy from batteries or the a.c. mains to other stores.
Heating devices transfer energy to thermal stores; motors transfer energy to kinetic stores.
Work is done when charge flows in a circuit.
E = P t: energy (J) = power (W) × time (s).
E = Q V: energy (J) = charge (C) × potential difference (V).
Energy transferred depends on the power of the appliance and how long it is on.
1 kW = 1000 W; 1 minute = 60 s; 1 hour = 3600 s.
1 V means 1 J of energy transferred per coulomb of charge.
Higher power rating means energy is transferred to useful stores faster.

keyTerms.definition: The movement of energy from one store to another, for example from the mains to the thermal store of water.
Energy transferred; when charge flows through a potential difference, work is done.
The rate at which an appliance transfers energy when operating normally, in watts.
Energy stored by a moving object, such as the turning parts of a motor.
Energy stored in an object because of its temperature.

workedExamples.title: Kilowatts and minutes
workedExamples.question: A 1.5 kW hair dryer is used for 4 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred.

workedExamples.title: Using E = Q V via Q = I t
workedExamples.question: A current of 0.50 A flows through a 9.0 V motor for 60 s. Calculate the energy transferred.
steps: Find the charge: Q = I t = 0.50 × 60 = 30 C.
Check: P = V I = 4.5 W and E = P t = 4.5 × 60 = 270 J.

workedExamples.title: Rearranging for time
workedExamples.question: A 600 W microwave oven transfers 54 000 J to some soup. Calculate how long it was on.
steps: Rearrange E = P t to t = E ÷ P.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a higher power appliance always transfers more energy.
misconceptions.right: In fact energy depends on power and time: a 100 W lamp left on for 10 hours transfers more energy than a 3000 W kettle on for 2 minutes.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often substitute minutes or hours directly into E = P t.
misconceptions.right: In fact time must be in seconds when power is in watts, so convert first.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think electricity itself is stored in the appliance.
misconceptions.right: In fact energy is transferred electrically by the moving charge and ends up in other stores, such as thermal or kinetic stores.

realWorld: Kettles, toasters, ovens and immersion heaters transfer energy to thermal stores; washing machines, fans and drills use motors to transfer energy to kinetic stores.
Battery-powered tools transfer energy from the chemical store of the battery to the kinetic store of the motor.
Choosing a lower power appliance, or using it for less time, reduces the energy transferred from the mains and so the electricity bill.
examTips: Decide which equation fits the data: E = P t if you know power and time; E = Q V if you know charge and potential difference.
Convert kW to W and minutes or hours to seconds before substituting.
For 'describe the energy transfer' questions, name the source (mains or battery), say energy is transferred electrically, and name the useful store (thermal or kinetic).
Large answers are fine: a kettle can easily transfer hundreds of thousands of joules. Give units, and use kJ or MJ if it helps.
summary: Appliances transfer energy from the mains or batteries to useful stores.
Heaters fill thermal stores; motors fill kinetic stores.
E = P t, with time in seconds.
E = Q V: potential difference is energy per coulomb.
Energy transferred depends on power and time switched on.
Convert kW to W and minutes or hours to seconds first.

questions.question: Which equation links energy transferred (E), power (P) and time (t)?
markScheme: 1 mark: E = P × t
questions.explanation: Energy transferred = power × time. A more powerful appliance or a longer time both transfer more energy.

questions.question: Which equation links energy transferred (E), charge flow (Q) and potential difference (V)?
markScheme: 1 mark: E = Q × V
questions.explanation: E = Q V. A potential difference of 1 V means 1 J is transferred per coulomb.

questions.question: Into which store does an electric kettle usefully transfer energy?
markScheme: 1 mark: Thermal store of the water
questions.explanation: The heating element raises the temperature of the water, increasing its thermal store.
options: Gravitational potential store of the kettle

questions.question: Into which store does the motor in a food mixer usefully transfer energy?
markScheme: 1 mark: Kinetic store
questions.explanation: Electric motors transfer energy to the kinetic store of the moving parts.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the power of four appliances and the time each one is switched on.
Which appliance transfers the most energy?
markScheme: 1 mark: Television
questions.explanation: Energy = P t with t in seconds: kettle 3000 × 60 = 180 000 J, toaster 1000 × 120 = 120 000 J, television 100 × 3600 = 360 000 J, LED lamp 10 × 3600 = 36 000 J. The low-power television on for a long time transfers the most energy.

questions.question: What is 2.5 kW in watts?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2500 W
questions.explanation: Multiply kilowatts by 1000: 2.5 × 1000 = 2500 W.

questions.question: Which statement describes a potential difference of 12 V?
markScheme: 1 mark: 12 J of energy is transferred per coulomb of charge
questions.explanation: Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge: 1 V = 1 J/C.
options: 12 C of charge flows each second
12 J of energy is transferred per coulomb of charge

questions.question:
Two heaters, A and B, are switched on for the same time. Heater A has twice the power of heater B.
Which statement is correct?
markScheme: 1 mark: A transfers twice as much energy as B.
questions.explanation: E = P t with the same t, so energy is proportional to power: twice the power, twice the energy.
options: A transfers half as much energy as B.
A transfers twice as much energy as B.
A transfers four times as much energy as B.

questions.question:
A 60 W lamp is switched on for 2 hours.
How much energy does the lamp transfer?
questions.explanation: 2 hours = 7200 s. E = 60 × 7200 = 432 000 J. 120 J comes from not converting hours to seconds.

questions.question:
A 2000 W kettle is switched on for 90 s.
Calculate the energy transferred by the kettle.

A 1.5 kW heater is switched on for 4.0 minutes.
Calculate the energy transferred by the heater.
markScheme: 1 mark: 1500 W and 240 s
questions.explanation: Convert both: 1.5 kW = 1500 W, 4.0 min = 240 s. E = 360 000 J.

questions.question:
30 C of charge flows through a 12 V lamp.
Calculate the energy transferred by the lamp.
markScheme: 1 mark: 360 J

questions.question:
A toaster connected to the 230 V mains supply transfers 4600 J of energy.
Calculate the charge that flows through the toaster.
markScheme: 1 mark: 20 C
questions.explanation: Rearrange E = Q V to Q = E ÷ V = 4600 ÷ 230 = 20 C.

questions.question:
A blender transfers 90 000 J of energy in 5.0 minutes.
Calculate the power of the blender.
markScheme: 1 mark: 5.0 min = 300 s
1 mark: 300 W
questions.explanation: Convert the time to seconds, then P = E ÷ t.

questions.question:
A heater connected to the 230 V mains supply has a current of 3.0 A for 2.0 minutes.
Calculate the energy transferred by the heater.
markScheme: 1 mark: 82 800 J
questions.explanation: Find the charge with Q = I t (time in seconds), then E = Q V. Alternatively P = V I = 690 W and E = P t = 690 × 120 = 82 800 J.

questions.question:
A 2.5 kW heater transfers 1.8 MJ of energy.
Calculate the time the heater was switched on.
Give your answer in minutes.
markScheme: 1 mark: 2500 W and 1 800 000 J
1 mark: 12 minutes
questions.explanation: Convert kW and MJ to W and J, find t = E ÷ P = 720 s, then divide by 60.

questions.question: Give two factors that affect the amount of energy transferred by an appliance.
markScheme: 1 mark: the power (rating) of the appliance
1 mark: how long it is switched on (time)
questions.explanation: E = P t, so both power and time matter.

questions.question: Describe the energy transfer that takes place in a battery-powered electric drill.
markScheme: 1 mark: from the chemical store of the battery
1 mark: transferred electrically (by the current / work done by charge)
1 mark: to the kinetic store of the motor/drill bit
questions.explanation: Source store, transfer pathway, useful store: chemical, electrical, kinetic.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by 'work is done when charge flows in a circuit'.
markScheme: 1 mark: energy is transferred (from the supply to the component)
1 mark: the amount is equal to charge × potential difference (E = Q V)
questions.explanation: Doing work means transferring energy. Charge moving through a potential difference transfers energy.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows information about a kettle and a fridge in a home.
A student says: 'The kettle always transfers more energy than the fridge.'
Evaluate the student's statement. Use data from Table 1 in your answer.
markScheme: 1 mark: energy depends on time as well as power (E = P t)
1 mark: the fridge is on for much longer (all day), so it may transfer more energy in total, e.g. 50 W × 24 h = 4.32 MJ versus 3 kW × 10 min = 1.8 MJ
questions.explanation: A low-power appliance running all the time can transfer more energy than a high-power one used briefly.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the inside of a hair dryer.
Describe the useful energy transfers in the hair dryer.
markScheme: 1 mark: energy transferred electrically to the heating element / thermal store (of the air)
1 mark: and to the kinetic store of the motor/fan
questions.explanation: A hair dryer contains both a heating element and a motor.

questions.question: Show that E = V I t, starting from E = Q V and Q = I t.
markScheme: 1 mark: substitute Q = I t into E = Q V
1 mark: E = (I t) × V = V I t
questions.explanation: Replacing Q with I t links the two energy equations, and also shows E = P t because P = V I.

questions.question: Describe, with examples, how different domestic appliances transfer energy from the mains supply or from batteries. Explain how the power rating of an appliance is related to the energy it transfers.
markScheme: Indicative content: when charge flows, work is done and energy is transferred electrically from the supply; mains comes from power stations (a.c.), batteries from their chemical store (d.c.); heating devices such as kettles, toasters and electric heaters transfer energy to thermal stores; devices with motors such as fans, drills, washing machines and food mixers transfer energy to kinetic stores; some, e.g. hair dryers, do both; some energy is dissipated to the surroundings (e.g. sound, heating of the casing); power rating is the energy transferred per second; E = P t; higher power transfers energy faster; for the same time, double the power means double the energy; total energy also depends on how long the appliance is on.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): several correct examples of both heating and motor appliances with correct stores, and a clear explanation of the link between power, time and energy using E = P t.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some correct examples and stores with a partial explanation of power.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one appliance or about power.
questions.explanation: Strong answers name the source, the useful store for each example, and use E = P t to link power to energy over a given time.

questions.question:
A kettle and a microwave oven are each used to heat a cup of water.
Table 1 shows the power of each appliance and the time it takes to heat the water.
Calculate the energy transferred by each appliance and suggest which is the better choice. Give a reason for your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: kettle: E = P t = 2000 × 40 = 80 000 J; microwave: E = 1200 × 75 = 90 000 J; the kettle has a higher power but is on for less time; the kettle transfers less energy in total for the same job, so it is more efficient / cheaper to run for this task; it is also faster; possible counterpoints: microwave heats in the cup directly, kettle may heat more water than needed.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both energies correctly calculated (with unit conversions) and a justified conclusion.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one correct calculation or a conclusion with limited support.
questions.explanation: Power alone does not tell you which uses more energy; E = P t shows the kettle transfers 80 kJ and the microwave 90 kJ.

questions.question: What is the unit of energy?
markScheme: 1 mark: Joule
questions.explanation: Energy is measured in joules. The watt is the unit of power (joules per second).

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how the energy transferred by a lamp changes with time.
Use Figure 1 to determine the power of the lamp.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct pair of values read from the graph, e.g. 1200 J in 30 s
questions.explanation: Rearrange E = P t to give P = E ÷ t. From the line, 1200 J is transferred in 30 s, so P = 1200 ÷ 30 = 40 W. Any point on the line gives the same answer, for example 2400 J in 60 s.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the potential difference across two appliances.
Compare the energy transferred by each coulomb of charge passing through the mains heater and through the car headlamp.
markScheme: 1 mark: each coulomb transfers 230 J in the heater and 12 J in the headlamp
1 mark: so each coulomb transfers about 19 times more energy in the mains heater (E = Q V)
questions.explanation: Potential difference is energy per unit charge, so with E = Q V and Q = 1 C, E equals the potential difference in joules.
